email.subject: Your parcel is waiting at the pick-up point

body.v: Your parcel is ready at the pick-up point. Collection is free.
At the counter, show the code displayed in your ParcelPoint app.

hotspots.explain: The address ends in parcelpoint.example, the carrier's domain.
"free": the exact opposite of a fee scam.
It sends you to an app you already have.
A plain "Hello", a little impersonal. Here, the domain settles it.

who.prompt: Who is really writing to you? Read the address, not just the name.
who.answer: ParcelPoint: the address is on its real domain, parcelpoint.example.
choices: A scammer with an almost identical address

emotion.prompt: Which feeling is this email pressing on?
emotion.answer: None. A calm notice, with no deadline and no pressure.
choices: None, it is a calm notice
Fear of the parcel being sent back
The wish to receive a gift

ask.prompt: What does it actually want you to do?
ask.answer: Go and collect your parcel. It is free, with no link and no sign-in.
choices: Collect the parcel, without paying anything
Pay a fee through a link

verify.prompt: How can you check through a channel you control?
verify.answer: Open the ParcelPoint app yourself: the pick-up point and your code are listed there.
choices: Reply to ask for the code
Forward the email to a friend

actions.label: Open the ParcelPoint app yourself and look at the pick-up details
actions.consequence: Your code and the pick-up point's address are right there.

actions.label: Collect the parcel with the code from your app
actions.consequence: Nobody asks you for money, and everything matches what the app shows.

actions.label: Reply to ask for the code
actions.consequence: Nobody reads replies to this notifications address. The code is in your app.

attacker_reveal: Bad luck for me: this one really is from ParcelPoint. Set it next to the "fee due" message: the real one costs nothing, has no link and sends you to the app. When nobody asks you for money, I have very little to work with.
